overview: This file brings together U.S. diplomatic reporting on Japanese maritime regulation and state support for shipping between 1933 and 1936. Its principal document is Vice Consul Robert Mills McClintock’s analysis of Japan’s new Law for the Safety of Vessels, accompanied by a complete English translation covering seaworthiness, load lines, wireless equipment, inspections, foreign vessels, penalties, and transitional provisions. Other documents concern Japanese shipbuilding and operating subsidies, opposition to international subsidy reductions, and a cross-reference to restrictions on foreign participation in the Dairen–Chosen coasting trade and a protest by the Texas Company.

subfiles.title: McClintock report on Japan’s new Law for the Safety of Vessels
subfiles.from: Vice Consul Robert Mills McClintock, Kobe
subfiles.about: An explanatory report assesses the operation and significance of Japan’s new maritime-safety legislation.
subfiles.summary: McClintock reports that Law No. 11 of March 14, 1933 took effect on March 1, 1934 and was designed partly to implement the 1930 International Load Line Convention. He comments on exemptions from wireless requirements, citing the loss of 65 lives when the Yashima Maru sank off Kobe, and discusses the roles of Lloyd’s Register and the Teikoku Kaiji Kyokai in ship classification. He also compares Japanese provisions with U.S. navigation law, notes the Japan Seamen’s Union’s support for crew-initiated inspections, and explains the law’s application to American vessels and certificates. The report closes with implementing ordinances and identifies Garnett, Cox, and Kawakita as sources.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: Translation of the Law for the Safety of Vessels
subfiles.from: Mercantile Marine Bureau, Department of Communications of the Japanese Government
subfiles.about: A complete English translation sets out Japan’s statutory system for vessel safety, inspection, certification, and enforcement.
subfiles.summary: The law requires Japanese vessels to remain seaworthy and regulates hulls, machinery, lifesaving equipment, sanitation, dangerous cargo, electrical installations, load lines, and wireless apparatus. It establishes periodical, intermediate, special-purpose, occasional, and construction inspections, while recognizing authorized classification societies for specified non-passenger vessels. Further articles govern certificates, detention, crew complaints, foreign vessels, treaty precedence, fines, bribery, collision prevention, and dangerous goods. Supplementary provisions repeal earlier maritime laws, create temporary exemptions, and prescribe the transition to the new inspection regime.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Dairen–Chosen coasting-trade restrictions
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to another file concerning restrictions on foreign vessels in the Dairen–Chosen coasting trade.
subfiles.summary: This filing note refers to document 895.801/1, sent from Seoul by Langdon to the Embassy at Tokyo. The referenced communication concerned foreign-vessel participation in the Dairen–Chosen coasting trade and a Texas Company protest after it was advised of limitations on such participation.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Japanese ship subsidies
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: A departmental memorandum summarizes a Kobe report on Japanese ship-construction and shipping-service subsidies.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes the Ship Construction Law effective October 1, 1932, which appropriated ¥11 million to remove 400,000 gross tons of obsolete shipping and construct 200,000 gross tons of fast cargo vessels. It tabulates service subsidies for 1930–1933 and identifies the principal recipients and routes, including N.Y.K., O.S.K., China, North and South America, Europe, Australia, and coastal services. It argues that Japan’s total subsidies were only one-fifth of those granted by the United States, despite Japan’s strong commitment to subsidies as an instrument of merchant-marine policy. The memorandum also records Japanese opposition to British proposals at the World Economic Conference and mentions Garrels’s projected subsidy schedule for 1934–1938.

interest: The file is especially useful because it combines the full translated statute with candid consular commentary about how the law worked in practice. McClintock’s discussion connects maritime safety to the Yashima Maru disaster, organized seamen, international conventions, foreign shipping, and the influence of the Mitsubishi and Mitsui interests over rival classification societies. The subsidy memorandum and Dairen–Chosen cross-reference broaden the picture from safety regulation to industrial policy, imperial coastwise trade, and the commercial problems encountered by foreign firms.
